passage:
Counsellor's note.

At the parents' meeting, Pooja's mother, Vasudha, told a group of relatives in the corridor, "My Pooja will be a doctor, you'll see." Pooja stood next to her smiling, but her hand was gripping her bag strap. Afterwards she came to see me. She said she enjoys the belief in her, and that it feels heavy too, especially with her chemistry marks slipping. She said she was tempted to hide the latest test result. We talked about telling her mother honestly instead. She decided to show Vasudha the paper that evening and say that the pride was lovely but sometimes it felt like a weight. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What did Vasudha tell the relatives in the corridor?
qa.a: "My Pooja will be a doctor, you'll see."

qa.q: What does Pooja's grip on her bag strap suggest, and what did she tell the counsellor?
qa.a: That she was tense while smiling. She said she enjoys her mother's belief, but it also feels heavy, especially with her chemistry marks slipping.

qa.q: What did Pooja decide to do instead of hiding her test result?
qa.a: Show the paper to her mother that evening and say honestly that the pride was lovely but sometimes felt like a weight.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Pooja tells her this?
qa.a: Probably surprised, maybe worried, but likely to want to help. She boasts because she is proud, so she may not have realised how heavy it felt.

grounding: A parent brags about the protagonist's future to relatives; she enjoys the belief but says honestly when it feels heavy.

passage:
Before. At Diwali, Pradeep's mother, Chandrika, told every aunty at the gathering, "Pradeep will crack the top engineering college, no doubt." He smiled and passed the sweets. His collar felt tight.

During. Three weeks later he got his half-yearly maths paper back: 41 out of 80. He folded it into his geometry box and did not show it to anyone. That night he lay awake picturing his mother's face at the next family call, telling everyone again. He thought about just not mentioning it, maybe forging the signature.

After. On Sunday morning, while she was chopping onions, he stood by the kitchen door. "Amma, I got 41 in maths. I didn't want to tell you. When you say those things to everyone, it feels really heavy. I like that you believe in me. I just can't carry all of it."

Chandrika put down the knife. She was quiet a long time. "I'll stop announcing things," she said. "Show me the paper. We'll find you help."

qa.q: What mark did Pradeep get in the half-yearly maths paper?
What might Pradeep have been worried about while he lay awake?
qa.a: He was anxious about disappointing his mother after she had boasted to everyone, and afraid of her face at the next family call.
Telling Amma the mark and saying the praise felt heavy worked, because it was honest, avoided hiding or forging, and let her respond with help.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see her own bragging after Pradeep speaks?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to realise her pride had become a burden for him, and decides to stop announcing things and help instead.

grounding: It shows a teen weighed down by a parent bragging about his future, tempted to hide a poor mark, who instead says honestly the pressure is too heavy.

passage:
Vaibhav, you think your Papa is too proud of you? Let me tell you about mine. I'm your Tarun Chacha, and when I was fifteen, my father told the whole mohalla I would be the first doctor in the family.

Every time he said it at the paan shop, I felt a stone on my chest. I was not a bad student, but I wasn't that good in chemistry. In Class 11 I failed the first unit test. Failed. I hid the answer sheet under my mattress for a month.

Then it came out at the parent-teacher meeting, in front of my father and my teacher. He didn't shout. He looked tired, and that was worse.

On the walk home I told him, "Baba, I love that you believe in me. But when you tell everyone I'll be a doctor, I feel I'm not allowed to fail." He stopped walking. After that, he still said he was proud of me, but he stopped announcing my future.

qa.q: Where did Tarun Chacha hide the answer sheet?
qa.a: He hid the answer sheet under his mattress for a month.

qa.q: What was young Tarun feeling each time his father bragged at the paan shop?
qa.a: He felt a heavy weight, like a stone on his chest, because he feared he could not live up to it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tarun Chacha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Telling his Baba on the walk home how heavy the praise felt was the turning point, because it replaced hiding with honesty and changed how his father talked.

qa.q: How did Tarun's father seem to feel at the parent-teacher meeting?
qa.a: He seemed tired and disappointed that his son had hidden the failure, more hurt by the secret than by the mark.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling a parent's bragging that felt like a weight, the harm of hiding a failed test, and saying honestly that the praise was too heavy.
